item.title: Nozawana Pickles: Nagano's Signature Pickled Greens — Guide
item.description: Nozawana are the long leafy greens of a local turnip variety originally from the Nozawa Onsen area, traditionally salt-pickled in large batches after the autumn harvest to preserve them through the long mountain winter, resulting in one of Nagano’s most characteristic tsukemono (pickles). The pickled greens have a savoury, gently tangy flavour and are eaten on their own, chopped over rice, wrapped around rice, or used as a filling for oyaki dumplings, appearing on tables and in shops throughout the prefecture as an everyday local staple.

item.title: Shinshu Miso: Japan's Most Widely Produced Miso — Guide
item.description: Shinshu miso, the rice-based miso produced in Nagano, is Japan’s most widely made variety, accounting for around half of all the country’s miso production, thanks to the region’s cool climate being ideal for the slow fermentation that gives it its characteristic golden colour and balanced, medium-salty flavour. Beyond seasoning countless dishes, the miso can be explored at breweries around the prefecture, some historic and centuries old, which offer tours, tastings and shops explaining the fermentation process behind this staple of Japanese cooking.

item.title: Shinshu Soba: Nagano's Celebrated Buckwheat Noodles — Guide
item.description: Shinshu soba (buckwheat noodles) is one of Nagano’s signature foods, the region’s cool climate, clean mountain water and buckwheat-friendly highland terrain making it one of Japan’s most celebrated soba-producing areas. The noodles are prized for their firm texture and rich, nutty buckwheat flavour, served cold with dipping sauce or hot in broth at countless restaurants across the prefecture, and many places also offer hands-on soba-making classes where visitors mix, roll, and cut their own noodles under a master’s guidance before eating them fresh.
